questions.prompt: Fictional Company X: 0.05 USD a share, 1,000 million shares. Fictional Company Y: 20 USD a share, 2 million shares. Which is bigger by market value?

options.text: Company Y, because its share price is 400 times higher
options.explanation: No: Y is 20 × 2 million = 40 million USD. Share price alone does not show size.
Right: 0.05 × 1,000 million = 50 million USD, against 40 million USD for Y.

options.text: They are the same size by market value
options.explanation: No: 50 million USD and 40 million USD are different.

questions.prompt: Simulated penny stock: bid 0.18, ask 0.20. You buy 10,000 shares and sell at once. What do you lose to the spread?

options.explanation: No: that is what you get back when you sell, 10,000 × 0.18.
No: that is what you paid, 10,000 × 0.20.

questions.prompt: A fictional company went from 80 million to 200 million shares in two years, then did a 1-for-10 reverse split. What is the most reasonable reading?

options.text: Repeated dilution plus a reverse split: check cash and financing first
options.explanation: Right: this pattern is a common warning sign that a company keeps funding itself by issuing shares.

options.text: The reverse split made holders 10 times richer
options.explanation: No: the share count fell by the same factor, so holders gained nothing from the split itself.

options.text: Holders lost 90% of their value, as they now hold a tenth of the shares
options.explanation: No: each share is now priced about 10 times higher, so the split itself leaves the value of the holding unchanged.

questions.prompt: Which group of signs most strongly suggests a possible pump and dump?

options.text: Paid promotion, no revenue, and insiders selling during the hype
options.explanation: Right: together these suggest the people behind the hype may be selling to new buyers.

options.text: Steady small revenue, on-time reports and very little daily trading
options.explanation: No: this describes a quiet, illiquid share. Liquidity is a risk, but this is not a pump pattern.

options.text: A share that trades over the counter and has a website
options.explanation: No: neither of these is a red flag on its own.

questions.prompt: You bought 3,000 shares at 0.50 with a stop at 0.45. The share is halted, then reopens at 0.30. Roughly what is the loss?

options.explanation: No: (0.50 − 0.45) × 3,000 = 150 is the plan. The stop could not fill during the halt.

options.text: About 600 USD, four times the plan
options.explanation: Right: (0.50 − 0.30) × 3,000 = 0.20 × 3,000 = 600 USD, four times the plan, and possibly worse in a thin market.
No: a halt pauses trading. Your position stays open.

questions.prompt: A small, honest-looking company files on time and has steady revenue, but trades only 5,000 shares a day. You want to buy 20,000. What is the best approach?

options.text: Buy all 20,000 at market, since the business looks sound
options.explanation: No: a sound business does not fix liquidity. Your order is 4 days of normal volume.

options.text: Treat it as a likely scam and report it to the regulator
options.explanation: No: nothing here suggests fraud. Not every small share is a scam.

options.text: Go much smaller, use limit orders, or stay out
options.explanation: Right: 20,000 ÷ 5,000 = 4 days of volume. Size down to what you could exit, or stay out.
